sector: Real Estate / Healthcare - Retirement Villages & Aged Care
overview: Summerset Group Holdings is one of New Zealand's largest retirement village developers and operators, building and managing a portfolio of 44 villages across New Zealand with a nascent but growing presence in Victoria, Australia (4 villages under development). Founded in 1997 and NZX-listed since 2011 (also ASX-listed as SNZ), the company operates under the Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) model: residents pay an upfront licence fee for the right to occupy a unit, and Summerset earns a Deferred Management Fee (DMF) upon exit — now 30% of the original ORA price for new NZ contracts, up from 25%, effective mid-August 2026. At FY2025 year-end (31 December 2025), total assets were NZ$9.2 billion, the portfolio comprised 8,673 total units, residents numbered 9,500+ and the land bank held 5,499 retirement units plus 1,173 care units across both countries.

business_model.summary: Capital-intensive ORA/DMF model where reported operating cash flow (OCF) is materially inflated by ORA receipts from residents — these are economically a financing flow (residents' loans of $3.3b on the balance sheet), not free cash flow. Management's preferred earnings measure is Underlying Profit, which strips out IFRS fair-value property revaluations and reinstates only realised development margins and resale gains. Revenue is predominantly recurring (care fees/village services ~62%, DMF income ~37%) but earnings quality depends heavily on: (1) new unit sales generating development margin, (2) resale activity generating resale gains, and (3) NZ residential property market conditions, which drive ORA pricing and resale velocity. In mid-August 2026 Summerset raised the NZ DMF rate from 25% to 30% for new contracts, estimated by the company to add ~NZ$35m of cash over five years; management reports no material impact on contracting rates in the subsequent two months.

revenue_streams.name: Care fees and village services
revenue_streams.notes: FY25: $223.6m, up 13% YoY. Includes care fees paid by residents and Health NZ ($55.7m in FY25), plus village weekly fees. Growing with portfolio size and care ORA conversion.

revenue_streams.name: Deferred management fees (DMF)
revenue_streams.notes: FY25: $137.2m, up 13% YoY. Earned on exit; rate raised from 25% to 30% (new NZ contracts, mid-August 2026), accruing over the same multi-year schedule. Growing as portfolio matures and resale volumes increase, now with a structurally higher take rate on new business.

business_model.ocf_note: Reported OCF of $548.2m in FY25 includes $746.6m of ORA receipts from new sales and resales, net of $220.4m repayments to departing residents. These net ORA flows ($526.2m) are residents' loans — a liability on the balance sheet — not income. True underlying operational cash generation is better proxied by Underlying Profit ($234.2m in FY25; $103.4m in H1-2026, down 3.0% YoY). CapEx was $722.4m in FY25, resulting in a net investment outflow of $174.2m (OCF minus CapEx) that is funded by debt.
business_model.customer_type: B2C — primarily retirees aged 70+ seeking independent living with continuum-of-care access. Health NZ (Te Whatu Ora) is a significant care fee payer ($55.7m in FY25, ~25% of care fee revenue).
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~94% of units delivered in FY25 (637 of 693). Portfolio spans 40 NZ villages across 11 regions, with no single region >20% of resales. Australia ~6% of FY25 deliveries (56 units). Four Victorian sites: Cranbourne North (open, first Australian aged care home operating — 72-bed facility, co-located continuum-of-care, accreditation process underway under the new Aged Care Act), Chirnside Park (open, strong pre-sales), Oakleigh South (under construction, FY27 deliveries), Torquay (under construction, FY27 deliveries).

main_competitors: Ryman Healthcare (RYM.NZ) — historically the largest NZ operator (~49 villages NZ/Australia). Financial recovery is now concrete, not just promised: FY26 results (reported ~August 2026) showed the first positive free cash flow in over a decade (NZ$188m), operating revenue +10% to NZ$849m, and applications exceeding turnover in Q4 FY26 for the first time since October 2024, driven substantially by the Australian aged care business. Ryman also raised its new-resident DMF to 30% and lifted weekly fees. Board has set a high bar for new developments and continues to sell non-core sites — selective growth rather than a return to its old expansion pace, but the turnaround narrative has shifted from balance-sheet survival to operating improvement.
Metlifecare — private NZ operator (~35 villages), taken private by EQT in 2021. No longer a listed competitor but a significant operational competitor for residents.
Oceania Healthcare (OCA.NZ) — listed NZX, care-heavy model. Smaller than Summerset, faces similar funding pressures.
Arvida Group (ARV.NZ) — formerly listed NZX, taken private by US infrastructure fund Stonepeak in 2024. Growth model focused on acquisitions; no longer a direct listed peer.
Bupa Care Services NZ — large private aged care and retirement village operator.
RetireAustralia / Lendlease / Aveo — major Australian operators in Summerset's target Victorian market.
competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'big two' actively growing listed NZ retirement village operators (the other being Oceania). Summerset claims the largest and most diverse land bank in the NZ retirement village sector. Leads NZ market on brand 'consideration' and 'first choice' metrics per internal surveys. Care centre occupancy 94% vs ~90% industry average. 91% village and 89% care resident satisfaction (FY25); 91%/88% maintained at H1-2026. Ryman's concrete operating recovery (positive FCF, rising applications) narrows the competitive gap that had opened up over 2023-2025 and should be monitored for intensifying competition for sites and residents into 2027.

moat_factors.description: 5,499-unit retirement land bank plus 1,173 care units across NZ and Australia — the largest in the NZ sector by management's claim. This multi-decade pipeline took years and significant capital to assemble and is not easily replicated by competitors. Includes consented sites across 11 NZ regions and 4 Victorian locations.

moat_factors.factor: Broadacre development model and in-house capability
moat_factors.description: Fully integrated in-house capability: land acquisition, planning, consenting, design, procurement and construction management. This enables: (a) cost discipline — FY25 development margin 27.8%, well above the 20-25% medium-term guidance (though H1-2026 realised development margin fell to 20%, the bottom of the range); (b) flexible build rate — Summerset can ramp up or down within quarters based on market conditions, as shown by the FY26 build-rate cut; (c) award-winning procurement (CIPS Australasia Best Procurement Transformation, 2025). Contrasts with Ryman, which has historically outsourced more and suffered cost overruns, though Ryman's FY26 recovery narrows this gap.

91% village and 89% care resident satisfaction (4-5 out of 5 scale), maintained through H1-2026 (91%/88%). Village NPS of 55, care NPS of 46. Seven consecutive years as Highly Commended Trusted Brand (Reader's Digest). Named Customer Champion by Australian Financial Review (2025). Staff retention 84% (well above sector average), eNPS 51 (top 5% of NZ healthcare providers). These metrics reinforce demand, pricing power, and care quality differentiation.

Residents make a significant capital commitment (average new ORA $693k) and face emotional and practical barriers to moving. DMF now accrues to 30% (new NZ contracts from mid-August 2026, up from 25%), incentivising longer stays further. Management reports contracting rates unaffected by the fee increase through the first two months, and notes the new rate is 'in line with comparable offerings across the sector' (Ryman independently moved to the same 30% new-resident rate). The model is capital-efficient for growth — ORA receipts from new residents partially fund construction of the next units.

44 NZ villages across 11 regions provides resilience to local property market weakness. Only 43% of FY25 resales came from Auckland/Wellington/Christchurch. Active in 22 locations across NZ and Australia. This allows prudent management of build rates by region and limits concentration risk. Q3-2026 showed Canterbury/Christchurch sales share rising (15% of Q3 sales vs 8% in Q2), evidence the regional diversification is functioning as a buffer.

Residents can move from independent living into care within the same village. Care ORA conversion programme significantly improved Care EBITDA from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25). Target of $20-25k care EBITDA per bed medium-term vs current ~$13k. First Australian continuum-of-care offering now operating at Cranbourne North (72-bed aged care home live, accreditation process underway).

weaknesses: Net debt rose to $2,058m at H1-2026 (from $1,960m at FY25 year-end) despite a stated deleveraging target; management's own debt band was reduced to $1.75b-$2.25b (from $2.0b-$2.5b), narrowing headroom even as the absolute level stays similar

Care business remains structurally underpowered: government funding increases consistently lag wage and operational cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff. The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group's August 2026 report calls for structural funding reform, but the government has not yet committed to a funding mechanism or timeline, so this remains unresolved

Australian operations are pre-revenue-at-scale and newly entering aged care operations for the first time (Cranbourne North) — execution and accreditation risk is real and immediate, not just prospective

Ryman's turnaround has moved from thesis to evidence (positive FY26 free cash flow, rising applications, 10% revenue growth) — a recovering, better-capitalised Ryman competing on the same 30% DMF rate reduces Summerset's relative differentiation and could intensify competition for new sites and residents sooner than previously assumed

ORA model concentrates revenue risk in a single NZ property market, and Q3-2026 already showed macro/geopolitical shock (Middle East conflict) denting new-sale volumes even as resales held up — confirming the demand-side sensitivity flagged in H1

growth_drivers: Demographic tailwind — the most powerful structural driver: NZ population aged 75+ is expected to double by 2048 and nearly triple over 50 years. Victoria, Australia's over-75 population expected to grow from ~550,000 today to ~1.2m over 40 years. Sector supply is structurally short of demand; NZ estimated to need 13,000 new aged care beds, with retirement villages expected to provide ~5,000.

Australia expansion gaining real momentum and now live in aged care: Cranbourne North village centre delivered and its 72-bed Australian aged care home is now operating (first time Summerset has run care outside NZ), working through accreditation under Australia's new Aged Care Act. Chirnside Park homes substantially pre-sold. Oakleigh South and Torquay under construction. Mornington permit lodged (fifth site). If Summerset replicates its NZ model, Australia effectively doubles the total addressable market, though FY26 NZ/total build guidance was cut in August, a reminder that execution timing can slip.

DMF rate increase to 30% (new NZ contracts, mid-August 2026) is a direct, structural uplift to future DMF income per unit with no observed demand offset through the first two post-announcement months — management estimates ~NZ$35m of additional cash over five years, and the move brings Summerset in line with Ryman's own 30% rate, suggesting an emerging sector-wide repricing rather than a Summerset-specific risk.

Care ORA conversion programme: converting standard care beds to ORA arrangements is significantly improving care profitability. Care EBITDA surged from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25); 767 further care units identified for conversion. Medium-term target of $20-25k care EBITDA per bed vs current ~$13k.

Portfolio maturation and compounding resale gains: as the portfolio grows and ages, resale volumes increase organically without requiring additional capital deployment. FY25: 755 resales (+16% YoY) generating $104.5m in realised gains across 32 villages. Momentum continued into FY26: resales were up 27% year-to-date through Q3-2026 and Q3 resales alone were up 36% YoY, even as new sales softened. Embedded value of $1.9b represents future cash when units turn over.

Land bank monetisation with deferred acquisition cost: 5,499-unit NZ and Australia land bank acquired at historic cost provides growth runway to almost double portfolio size. FY26 NZ build guidance was cut in August to 600-650 homes (from 650-700); group medium-term build rate held at 600-700 p.a. Consenting programme progressing — resource consents received for Rotorua, Mosgiel, Belmont (Auckland).

Interest rate normalisation tailwinds: RBNZ has cut the OCR significantly from its prior peak. Lower rates reduce finance costs on debt, improve NZ property market conditions (supporting higher ORA pricing and resale velocity — visible in the strong resale trend through Q3-2026), and expand investment property valuations (supporting NTA growth). Summerset is operationally leveraged to a falling rate environment.

Technology and operational efficiency investments: Lumin resident platform rolling out to all villages in FY26, remote National Clinical Support (NCS) nursing service expanding to all NZ care centres, AI transcription and care-insight tools piloted, robotics deployed across villages — compounding efficiency improvements that reduce cost per resident over time; corporate overhead cost per unit already down 6% since FY25.

business.risk: NZ residential property market downturn / macro shocks reducing ORA pricing and new-sale velocity
business.description: Summerset's DMF income, development margin, NTA and IFRS earnings are all linked to NZ residential property values and buyer confidence. The Q3-2026 sales update confirmed new sales fell versus Q3-2025, which management attributed to prospective residents hesitating to list their homes amid the Middle East conflict — directly analogous to the April/early-May 'Iran fuel crisis' dip flagged at H1. Resales, by contrast, grew strongly (+36% YoY in Q3, +27% YTD), suggesting the existing resident base is turning over well even while new-to-village demand is more exposed to macro sentiment shocks. The pattern of repeated, event-driven dips in new sales over 2026 raises the question of whether this is noise or an emerging sensitivity to global instability.

business.risk: Uncontracted stock accumulation and slow sell-down
business.description: As at FY25 year-end, 541 new units and 208 resale units were available for sale (9.7% of portfolio). Metro Auckland and Wellington villages have above-normal apartment stock to sell through. Q3-2026 contract data showed new-sale contracts up 20% on Q1/Q2-2026 levels (though flat vs Q3-2025) and resale contracts also up versus Q1/Q2, evidence of improving sell-through momentum into Q4, but settlement timing remains dependent on the housing market.

Government funding rates (Health NZ) for residential care consistently increase below actual wage and operational cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff. Care EBITDA per bed in completed villages is ~$13k vs the $20-25k medium-term target. The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group (chaired by David Cunliffe) released its report, 'A place to grow old: Securing the future of aged care,' on 18 August 2026 with 40 recommendations calling for structural funding reform, a needs-based funding model, and a reset of resident contributions. The government has directed the Ministry of Health to work through the recommendations but has not committed to a funding mechanism, cost, or implementation timeline. This remains an unresolved, binary-ish catalyst: a funded reform could be a material care-margin tailwind, but there is no confirmed date or dollar commitment yet.

business.risk: Construction cost inflation and development margin compression
business.description: FY25 development margin of 27.8% was above the 20-25% medium-term guidance range due to a favourable villa-heavy mix. H1-2026 realised development margin fell to 20%, the bottom of the guided range, as more care centres and apartment suites settled — confirming management's own guidance that margins would normalise down. FY26 guidance remains 20-25%. Sustained cost inflation could erode margins further if ORA pricing (including the new 30% DMF) does not fully offset it.

financial.risk: Debt band reduced while net debt keeps rising
financial.description: Net debt rose to $2,058m at H1-2026 (from $1,960m at FY25 year-end), driven by a $85.3m development outflow and ~$25m of AUD FX translation, even as management narrowed its target debt band to $1.75b-$2.25b (from $2.0b-$2.5b) and set a goal of net debt below $1.9b and gearing at 33% by end-2027. Gearing was 36.9% at H1-2026 against the 30-40% band. The combination of a tighter band and a rising absolute debt figure leaves less margin for error than the headline FY25 story suggested, and the end-2027 deleveraging target depends on execution (slower build rate, DMF increase, Australia capex tapering) all landing roughly on schedule.

financial.risk: OCF inflation masking true cash generation
financial.description: Reported OCF of $548.2m in FY25 (and the FY26 guided $50-70m 'cash flow from existing operations,' up from $32.3m in FY25) is meaningfully inflated by net ORA inflows which represent residents' loans on the balance sheet, not free cash flow. True operational cash generation is better proxied by Underlying Profit, which fell 3.0% YoY in H1-2026 to $103.4m. With continued heavy CapEx guided at $375-425m for FY26, the business continues to consume materially more cash than it earns operationally, funded by debt.

financial.risk: Prior-period restatement of investment property accounting
financial.description: The H1-2026 interim report disclosed two corrections of error: investment property fair value had not correctly accounted for loans to residents under NZ IAS 40 (overstating investment property and fair value gains), and the timing of derecognition of residents' loans for transferring residents changed. Restated comparatives: H1-2025 NPAT fell from $127.2m to $89.4m, equity from $3,173.5m to $3,110.8m, and NTA from 1318.44c to 1292c. No effect on cash flows, banking covenants, revenue or underlying profit, but it is a reminder that the IFRS fair-value layer of these accounts carries real technical complexity and historical error risk.

Growing Australian operations create NZD/AUD translation exposure, which contributed ~$25m to the net debt increase at H1-2026 via FX translation. Immaterial relative to the balance sheet overall but will grow as Australia expands toward its FY27 build targets.

regulatory.risk: NZ Retirement Villages Act Amendment Bill
regulatory.description: As of early November 2026 the Bill has still not been introduced to Parliament; legal commentary through mid-2026 continued to describe introduction as expected 'later this year,' with a Select Committee process to follow introduction. No first reading has been confirmed in available sources. Key proposed changes remain as previously flagged: mandatory cessation of weekly fees immediately after a resident vacates; no charging for operator-owned chattel maintenance; interest payable to outgoing residents after 6 months if their unit remains unsold; mandatory buy-back/repayment within 12 months post-vacate if unsold. Summerset states its practices already substantially align. The slippage in timing (from a 'July 2026' expectation to still-not-introduced by November) reduces near-term urgency but leaves the eventual mandatory buy-back liquidity risk unresolved and unquantified pending the actual Bill text and transition provisions.

regulatory.risk: Australian Aged Care Act compliance and operational readiness
regulatory.description: Australia's new Aged Care Act came into force on 1 November 2025. Summerset's Cranbourne North 72-bed aged care home is now open and operating, with the company working through staffing, training and accreditation under the new Act (no star rating yet, as is normal in the first 12 months of operation). This is now a live operational risk rather than a future one: any compliance failure, staffing shortfall, or accreditation delay at this flagship first-mover site could damage the brand at a critical moment in the Australian market entry and delay the path to the 300 units/year target.

regulatory.risk: Aged care sector funding model reform
regulatory.description: The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group reported on 18 August 2026 (ahead of its original June 2026 target having slipped, but still materially earlier than previously tracked in this analysis) with 40 recommendations for structural reform, including a needs-based funding model and reset resident contributions. Minister for Seniors Casey Costello confirmed the Ministry of Health has been directed to work through the recommendations with other agencies; no funding commitment, cost, or implementation date has been announced. This remains the single most consequential unresolved policy catalyst for Summerset's and the sector's care economics — positive reform with real funding could materially lift the $13k-vs-$20-25k per-bed EBITDA gap; continued delay or a watered-down response perpetuates the status quo.

macro.risk: Interest rate movements and NZ economic conditions
macro.description: After the RBNZ cut rates significantly from its 2023-24 peak, the NZ economic environment showed early recovery signs through 2026, visible in strong resale momentum (+27% YTD through Q3). Lower interest rates benefit Summerset both directly (lower finance costs) and indirectly (improved NZ property market, better retiree ability to sell homes). However, any stalling of the rate-cutting cycle, or renewed global instability (as seen in the Q3 new-sales dip), would re-tighten both channels.

macro.risk: NZ and Australian construction cost and labour inflation
macro.description: Operating expenses grew 16% in FY25 to $328.6m, driven by employee costs (58% of opex), with healthcare wages rising faster than government funding increases. NZ construction and healthcare labour markets remain tight. Summerset partially mitigates through procurement discipline and standardised designs, with corporate overhead per unit down 6% since FY25, but sustained above-CPI labour inflation remains a persistent earnings headwind, especially in care operations.

macro.risk: Geopolitical shocks affecting consumer confidence and settlement timing
macro.description: Two consecutive events in 2026 (the April/early-May fuel-price shock linked to Iran, and Middle East conflict uncertainty affecting Q3 new sales) have each independently dented new-sale volumes by making prospective residents hesitant to list their own homes for sale. While each was described by management as an isolated, non-recurring quarter effect with no flow-on, the repetition across two separate quarters in the same year suggests retiree home-sale decisions may be more sensitive to macro/geopolitical headline risk than previously modelled, even though resales (the existing resident base) have been resilient throughout.

macro.risk: Australian property market and demand execution
macro.description: Summerset is entering the Victorian retirement village market without an established long track record, though early signals (strong Chirnside Park pre-sales, Cranbourne North care home now operating) are encouraging. Melbourne's apartment and property market conditions through 2026-2027 will continue to influence ORA pricing and sales velocity at the newer sites.

execution.description: Summerset delivered only 56 Australian units in FY25 and guided 100-150 for FY26. Reaching ~300/year by end of FY27 requires simultaneous scaling across 4+ sites in an unfamiliar regulatory, labour and market environment, while now actually operating (not just planning) aged care for the first time in Australia at Cranbourne North. Accreditation, staffing, and the transition from a construction-partner model to in-house self-management all remain live execution items. Cost overruns or demand shortfalls could impair returns and delay Australia's contribution to group earnings.

execution.risk: Village centre build programme complexity and delivery concentration
execution.description: FY25 had the highest ever number of simultaneous commercial builds. Several more NZ village centre buildings are due through FY26-FY27. Village centres contain care centres, serviced apartments and amenities — more complex and lower-margin than villas, as evidenced by H1-2026's realised development margin falling to the bottom of the guided range. The FY26 NZ and total build guidance cut (announced with H1-2026 results) reflects management actively managing this complexity by slowing the pace rather than pushing through delivery risk.

New CFO Margaret Warrington joined February 2025. Sales and marketing leadership roles were consolidated under David Martin (formerly Metlifecare) from January 2026. No further senior leadership changes have been identified since the H1-2026 result. Execution through the Q3-2026 sales softness (handled with a published, confident outlook commentary) suggests the newer commercial leadership structure is operating normally, though this is early evidence only.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ retirement village sector has strong secular demand tailwinds: the over-75 population is set to double by 2048. Industry supply has historically been insufficient to meet demand growth (NZ estimated to need ~13,000 additional aged care beds, with retirement villages providing ~5,000). NZ property market showed early recovery signs through 2026, supported by RBNZ rate cuts, though new-sale volumes remain sensitive to macro/geopolitical sentiment shocks (two such dips occurred in 2026). Sector-wide competitive intensity, which had fallen as Ryman paused development and Arvida went private, is now showing early signs of rebuilding as Ryman's FY26 results confirm a genuine operational and cash-flow recovery (first positive FCF in a decade, rising applications). Both Summerset and Ryman have independently moved new-resident DMF rates to 30%, suggesting a broader sector repricing rather than a company-specific move. Australia (Victoria specifically) remains a large greenfield opportunity, now moving from construction to live operations (Cranbourne North aged care). The NZ Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group's August 2026 report puts structural care-funding reform squarely on the government's agenda, though with no committed timeline or mechanism yet, and the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill has still not been introduced to Parliament as of early November 2026.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high cyclicality tied to residential property market and, as 2026 has shown, to macro/geopolitical sentiment shocks affecting prospective new residents' willingness to list their homes. Business fundamentals (DMF, care fees) are relatively stable and provide a floor, strengthened further by the 25%->30% DMF increase. Resale activity has proven more resilient than new sales through 2026's shocks (resales +27% YTD vs new sales softening in Q3), suggesting the existing resident turnover cycle is a more stable earnings stream than new-to-village demand.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — dual sensitivity: (1) Rising rates increase finance costs on debt directly; (2) Higher rates reduce NZ property market activity, slowing ORA sales as retirees struggle to sell existing homes. RBNZ rate cuts through 2024-2026 remain a meaningful tailwind, visible in strong resale momentum. Management targets gearing of 33% and net debt below $1.9b by end-2027 as the portfolio matures and Australia passes its peak capex phase.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Limited but growing AUD/NZD exposure as Australian operations scale; contributed ~$25m to the H1-2026 net debt increase via FX translation. All reporting in NZD. Currently modest (~6-10% of deliveries in Australia) but will grow toward management's ~25-30% of deliveries by end of FY27 target.
key_input_costs: Healthcare labour (nurses, caregivers) — largest operating cost at 58% of opex ($190.6m in FY25); exposed to minimum wage and sector wage inflation well above the level of government funding increases
Construction materials (concrete, steel, timber) — standardised designs, EC30 reduced-carbon concrete standard, and mature procurement programmes partially mitigate inflation
Insurance and council rates — both increasing above CPI; property-related expenses $33.6m in FY25 (10% of opex)
Energy costs — accelerating transition to solar and away from gas to reduce exposure

recent_developments.event: Q3-2026 sales of occupation rights update (quarter ended 30 September 2026, released ~12 October 2026). Total sales 415 (175 new, 240 resales). Year-to-date (nine months) sales 1,228, up 10% on 9M-FY25; resales up 27% YTD. Q3 resales up 36% YoY and ahead of Q2's 227. New sales were DOWN on Q3-2025, attributed to prospective residents hesitating to sell their homes amid Middle East conflict uncertainty -- the same demand-dampening dynamic flagged for the April/early-May 'Iran fuel crisis' dip at H1, now recurring in a second quarter. Canterbury/Christchurch share of sales rose to 15% of Q3 (from 8% in Q2). New-sale contracts in Q3 were up 20% on Q1/Q2-2026 (but flat vs Q3-2025); resale contracts up on Q1/Q2 and well ahead of Q3-2025. No settlement figures or formal guidance changes were given in this release; management says sales activity has improved since June and it enters Q4 with a 'solid pipeline' and is managing the development programme 'with discipline.' Company also confirmed no material change in contracting rates following the mid-August DMF increase to 30%, describing the new rate as in line with sector norms.

DEFERRED MANAGEMENT FEE INCREASED from 25% to 30% for new NZ ORA contracts, announced mid-August 2026 (around the time of the H1-2026 result). Company estimates the change adds ~NZ$35m of cash over five years. This is a direct structural increase to future DMF income per unit. Ryman Healthcare has separately also moved new-resident DMF to 30%, pointing to a broader sector repricing.

Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group released its report 'A place to grow old: Securing the future of aged care' on 18 August 2026 -- chaired by Hon David Cunliffe, 40 recommendations for structural reform including a needs-based funding model and a reset of resident contributions to the cost of care. Minister for Seniors Casey Costello confirmed the Ministry of Health has been directed to work through the recommendations with other agencies; no funding commitment, mechanism, or implementation timeline has been announced as of early November 2026. This report landed just before (and was not reflected in) the prior 2026-08-28 analysis refresh, which still described it as 'expected June 2026.' THESIS-RELEVANT: this is the single most consequential pending policy catalyst for care-segment economics and should be tracked closely for the government's formal response.

H1-2026 result (six months to 30 June 2026). Underlying profit $103.4m, DOWN 3.0% on H1-2025's $106.6m -- the first half-on-half decline in the series. Statutory NPAT of $171.4m (+91.7%) is not comparable: it reflects a $191.1m investment-property fair value movement against a restated base. Revenue $200.3m (+15.7%). Total ORA sales 813 units (398 new, 415 resales). Retirement units in portfolio 7,458; care units 1,696. Interim dividend 3.8cps. NTA $14.41/share.

PRIOR-PERIOD RESTATEMENT disclosed in Note 1 of the H1-2026 interim report -- two corrections of error. (a) Investment property fair value did not correctly account for loans to residents under NZ IAS 40, overstating investment property and fair value gains. (b) The timing of derecognition of residents' loans for transferring residents changed. Restated comparatives: H1-2025 NPAT $127.2m -> $89.4m, equity $3,173.5m -> $3,110.8m, NTA 1318.44c -> 1292c; FY2025 total assets $9,234.9m -> $9,294.2m. No effect on cash flows, banking covenants, revenue or underlying profit.

FY26 GUIDANCE CUT on build rate. NZ deliveries now 600-650 homes (previously 650-700) and total 700-800 (previously 750-850); medium-term group build rate held at 600-700 p.a. Management explicitly flagged that lower sales rates in April and early May, in reaction to the Iran fuel crisis, mean Q3-2026 settlements were forecast DOWN on prior periods -- described as an isolated quarter with no expected flow-on to Q4 (the subsequent October sales update showed new sales did soften again in Q3, though for a related but distinct reason -- Middle East conflict uncertainty rather than the earlier fuel crisis). Cash flow from existing operations guided $50-70m (FY25: $32.3m). Construction capex $375-425m. Development margin 20-25%, in line with medium-term guidance.

Balance sheet: net debt $2,058m at 1H26, UP from $1,960m at FY25 despite the deleveraging target, driven by $85.3m development outflow and ~$25m AUD FX translation. Gearing 36.9% against a 30-40% band; company targets 33% and net debt below $1.9b by end-2027. Target debt range REDUCED to $1.75b-$2.25b (previously $2.0b-$2.5b). Corporate overhead cost per unit down 6% since FY25.

Operating metrics held up: village resident satisfaction 91% (every village at or above the 80% target, 24 villages above 90%), care satisfaction 88% with all care centres at a positive NPS. Occupancy lifting in new villages; retirement village occupancy target 95%. Cranbourne North (first Australian continuum-of-care village) officially opened, with its 72-bed aged care home co-located and beginning to operationalise under Australia's new Aged Care Act (hiring, training, accreditation under way).

Investor Day held 1 May 2026 at Cranbourne North, Australia's first Summerset village -- covered progress at Chirnside Park and Oakleigh South and reinforced the Australian growth narrative ahead of the H1 result.

Summerset Annual General Meeting held online only on 21 April 2026 (originally planned in-person at Wellington) due to Wellington state of emergency following extreme rainfall and flash flooding. No significant governance or strategic changes announced at AGM.

Final FY2025 dividend of 13.2 cents per share paid on 26 March 2026 (record date 12 March 2026). Full year FY25 dividend of 24.5 cps, flat on FY24, represents 25.3% of underlying profit. Board formally adopted three-year review cycle for dividend policy; policy to be reviewed during FY26.

FY2025 full year results released (27 February 2026): Record underlying profit $234.2m (+13% on FY24), record 1,560 ORA sales (+26% on FY24), 693 units delivered (637 NZ + 56 Australia), NTA $13.75/share (+$1.32 YoY), total assets $9.2b (+15%). IFRS net profit $259.7m (down 22% on FY24 due to lower fair value movements vs prior year, later restated downward further per the H1-2026 Note 1 correction). Total debt $1.97b (vs $2.0-2.5b target band then in force).

David Martin joined as Chief Sales and Marketing Transformation Lead, consolidating previously separate sales and marketing ELT roles. Martin brings experience from Metlifecare, where he led the commercial transformation and rebrand.

guidance.caveat: Q3-2026 settlements were pre-warned down at H1 due to the April/early-May 'Iran fuel crisis' sales dip; the October Q3 sales release (not a settlements figure) subsequently confirmed Q3 new sales were again down YoY, this time attributed to Middle East conflict uncertainty, while resales were strong (+36% YoY). Management describes both dips as isolated/transitory and says it enters Q4 with a solid pipeline, but no formal FY26 guidance was reaffirmed or revised in the October release -- the FY26 targets set at H1 (as of 2026-08-28) remain the most recent formal guidance on record.

bull_case: Demographic demand is the most powerful structural growth driver in the NZ-listed universe: NZ's 75+ population doubles by 2048 while sector supply structurally undershoots demand. Summerset's 5,499-unit land bank pipeline was assembled at historical cost and provides a multi-decade delivery runway at minimal incremental land cost. This is a near-irreplaceable competitive asset.

The DMF rate increase to 30% (mid-August 2026) is a clean, demand-neutral-so-far structural earnings uplift: management reports no material impact on contracting rates two months post-increase, and Ryman's parallel move to 30% suggests this is sector-wide repricing power rather than a one-off Summerset decision that could be competed away.

Australia is now genuinely operating, not just building: Cranbourne North's village centre and its first Australian aged care home (72 beds) are live, Chirnside Park is substantially pre-sold, and Oakleigh South/Torquay are under construction with a fifth site (Mornington) in planning. If Summerset replicates even a fraction of its NZ model success in Victoria, the long-run earnings power is substantially underpriced at current NTA-based valuations.

Resale gains are a compounding, capital-light flywheel that has proven resilient through 2026's macro shocks: resales were up 27% year-to-date through Q3-2026 (+36% in Q3 alone) even as new-sale volumes softened twice during the year on unrelated geopolitical shocks. As the portfolio matures, this stream grows organically without requiring further land or build investment.

The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group's August 2026 report puts structural care-funding reform formally on the government's agenda for the first time with a detailed 40-point blueprint; any meaningful funded response would directly close Summerset's $13k-vs-$20-25k per-bed care EBITDA gap and is a call option not yet priced in, since no mechanism or cost has been announced.
bear_case: Net debt kept rising through H1-2026 ($2,058m, up from $1,960m at FY25) even as management narrowed its own target debt band to $1.75b-$2.25b (from $2.0b-$2.5b) -- the balance sheet has less real headroom than the FY25 narrative implied, and the end-2027 deleveraging target (33% gearing, sub-$1.9b net debt) depends on multiple levers (slower builds, the DMF increase, Australian capex tapering) all executing roughly on schedule.

New-sale demand has now softened in two separate quarters of 2026 for two separate macro/geopolitical reasons (the April/May fuel-price shock, then Middle East conflict uncertainty in Q3) -- a pattern that raises the question of whether retiree home-sale decisions are more macro-sensitive than previously assumed, even though resales have so far absorbed the shock.

Ryman Healthcare's turnaround has moved from thesis to evidence: FY26 brought Ryman's first positive free cash flow in over a decade (NZ$188m), 10% revenue growth, and applications exceeding turnover for the first time since October 2024. A better-capitalised, operationally improving Ryman charging the same 30% DMF reduces Summerset's competitive differentiation and could intensify competition for sites and residents sooner than the 'reduced competition' thesis assumed as recently as mid-2026.

The Retirement Villages Amendment Bill's mandatory 12-month buy-back obligation remains unresolved and has still not been introduced to Parliament as of November 2026, well past the 'mid-2026'/'by July 2026' expectations repeatedly cited through the year -- the delay removes near-term clarity but leaves the eventual liquidity-risk mechanics (and systemic sector-supply risk if smaller operators exit) an open-ended overhang rather than a resolved, quantifiable item.

IFRS earnings remain volatile, and the H1-2026 prior-period restatement (correcting an IAS 40 investment-property/resident-loan accounting error that cut H1-2025 NPAT from $127.2m to $89.4m and NTA from 1318.44c to 1292c) is a reminder that the fair-value layer of these accounts carries real technical complexity and historical error risk, on top of the usual swings driven by external property valuers' assumptions.
analysis_note_2026_08_28: Narrative refreshed on the H1-2026 result. The headline to carry into any valuation: underlying profit -- the measure this business is valued on -- went BACKWARDS 3.0%, while statutory NPAT nearly doubled on a fair-value movement against a restated base. Anyone reading the +91.7% NPAT line as growth is reading an accounting artefact. Build guidance was cut and Q3 settlements are pre-warned lower.
analysis_note_2026_11_02: Narrative-only refresh, no new filings (next scheduled filing is the FY2026 annual result, expected ~February 2027). Nothing found that rises to a corporate-action level (no takeover, equity raise, delisting, or major guidance revision) and the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill still has NOT been introduced to Parliament as of this date -- commentary continues to describe it as 'expected later in 2026' with no first reading confirmed, so this remains an open overhang, not a resolved one. Four developments are worth carrying into the next DCF touch, none individually large enough to warrant an immediate re-run on their own, but collectively worth a sensitivity check: (1) the DMF rate increase to 25%->30% on new NZ contracts (mid-August 2026, ~NZ$35m/5yr per company estimate, apparently demand-neutral so far) is a genuine structural uplift to future DMF revenue per unit -- if durable, this nudges the DMF assumption in the model up, not down; (2) the Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group's 40-recommendation report landed 18 August 2026 (slightly ahead of the 'June 2026' expectation carried in the prior note, but with no government funding commitment or timeline yet) -- this is the single most consequential pending catalyst for the care-segment margin assumption and should be watched for the government's formal response, not yet actioned; (3) Ryman Healthcare's FY26 results (first positive FCF in a decade, +10% revenue, applications exceeding turnover) confirm the competitive-reprieve assumption embedded in the bull case is time-limited -- a risk-weight check on the 'reduced competition' growth driver is warranted at the next full refresh; (4) the Q3-2026 sales update (new sales down YoY on Middle East conflict uncertainty, resales up 36% YoY) is the second macro-shock-driven new-sales dip of the year and supports keeping the build-rate/new-sales growth assumption conservative near the low end of guidance rather than assuming a snap-back, while the resale/DMF stream can reasonably be modelled as resilient. None of this moves WACC. Recommend the dcf-analyst treat this as a watch-list update rather than a trigger for revising build rate, margin, or discount rate inputs this cycle.
